title: Sequential Outlier Detection in Non-Stationary Time
Sequential Outlier Detection in Non-Stationary Time Series
summary: The paper addresses sequential outlier detection in time series whose mean can drift, where repeated tests inflate false-positive probabilities. It estimates the mean with a one-sided local-linear smoother plus Jackknife bias reduction, then uses extreme-value theory to set GEV-based critical values for the maximum residual over n consecutive tests. In simulations and Australian temperature data, the full and partial procedures achieve high specificity and competitive sensitivity, with the full IID μ1 n=50 standard-normal setting reporting 98.3% specificity.

why: The authors' repository contains a pure NumPy/SciPy implementation of the proposed full method (called 'sequential' in code), and C1 is a synthetic no-outlier simulation cell that needs no external data or weights. The core run should work on Python 3.12 after installing standard scientific packages and avoiding optional competitor-method imports (rpy2/tensorflow/river), which are not needed for C1.
est_runtime: About 10-15 minutes with 22-core parallelization over series; roughly 25-30 minutes if the authors' code is run single-process.
blockers: No requirements.txt/pyproject; core dependencies must be installed manually (numpy, scipy, pandas, matplotlib, tueplots).
alternative_methods.py imports optional rpy2/tensorflow/river for competitor methods; these are not needed for C1 and may be unavailable on Windows/Python 3.12.

approach: Reproduce the matched target C1 only: the proposed full method on 1,000 no-outlier IID standard-normal series rescaled to mean 0 and sd 1/20, mean function μ1, n=50, horizon 11n=550. The implementation will be a thin wrapper around the authors' pure NumPy/SciPy code, calling experiments.sequential_test (the code's name for the full method) and data_generation.py for μ1 rather than rewriting the estimator. reproduce.py will seed all stochastic steps, parallelize over series, pool decisions on indices n+1..11n, compute 100*TN/(TN+FP), and write results/metrics.json checked against 98.3% ± 1.0 percentage point. Optional C2-C5 can reuse the same wrapper only if the C1 run finishes well inside budget; C6-C8 need external BOM data and are out of scope for the matched target.
steps: Clone the authors' repository if it is not already present: git clone https://github.com/FlorianHeinrichs/outlier_detection.git and cd into it.

Install core dependencies with python -m pip: numpy scipy pandas matplotlib tueplots tqdm. Do not install or import competitor stacks for C1 unless required by an author import; if experiments.py imports alternative_methods and that fails on optional rpy2/tensorflow/river, add a minimal sys.modules/import shim in reproduce.py or c1_runner.py rather than editing author files.

Inspect experiments.py, data_generation.py, experiments_config.py, jackknife.py, and quantiles.py to read exact function signatures, the μ1 generator, default bandwidth grid, GEV fitting code, and whether sequential_test is the full method. Record the actual call signature in c1_runner.py.

Implement c1_runner.py: a function run_one_series(series_seed) that calls the authors' data generator for μ1 with IID N(0,1) errors rescaled to mean 0 and sd 1/20, no outliers, length 550; calls experiments.sequential_test with alpha=0.01, full estimator, quartic kernel, 5-fold CV bandwidth; returns a boolean rejection array for indices n+1..11n.

Implement reproduce.py: parse --smoke (5 series) versus default (1000 series); set base seed 0 and deterministic per-series seeds; parallelize over series with multiprocessing.Pool using an if __name__ == '__main__' guard; collect rejection counts.

Run a smoke test on 5 series before touching the full run: python reproduce.py --smoke. Confirm data shapes, finite residuals, finite GEV fits, a selected bandwidth inside the grid, and exactly 5*500=2500 test decisions.
Run the full C1 experiment with python reproduce.py. Use min(16, cpu_count) workers; save optional per-series rejection counts to results/c1_per_series.csv for audit.
Aggregate specificity by pooling all normal test decisions: specificity_percent = 100 * (1 - total_rejections / (n_series * (11*n - n))). For C1 the denominator is 1000*500 = 500,000 test points.

Write results/metrics.json with claim_id C1, metric specificity_percent, value, paper_value 98.3, tolerance_abs 1.0, unit %, n, horizon, n_series, test_points, alpha, seed, runtime, selected-bandwidth summary, and status reproduced/not_reproduced if abs(value-98.3)<=1.0.

Check the tolerance. If outside 1.0 point, run diagnostics only: verify full-vs-partial function choice, GEV shape sign, use of rolling vs disjoint maxima, exclusion of first n from the metric, bandwidth CV split, and seed handling. Do not tune undocumented choices to hit the paper value; document any unresolved discrepancy.

If C1 passes and more than 15 minutes remain, optionally run C2-C5 via the same wrapper with n=200 or contaminated settings using A7 for outlier heights. Otherwise stop; C6-C8 are out of scope because they require external BOM data.
smoke_test: python reproduce.py --smoke. This runs 5 series, n=50, horizon=550, no outliers, and should finish in about 1-2 minutes on CPU. Success criteria: generated series are finite and length 550; GEV fit finite; selected bandwidth is within the configured grid; exactly 2500 rejection decisions are produced; results/metrics.json is written. The smoke specificity is not required to be within 1.0 of 98.3, only the data flow must be proven.
intermediate_checks: After install, verify imports without competitor stacks: python -c "import experiments, data_generation; print('ok')" after any optional-import shim; if this fails, resolve import errors before writing the runner.
Confirm in experiments.py that sequential_test is the full all-observations-up-to-i method and partial_test is the partial method; the README wording is ambiguous, so check the code/docstring.
Generate one μ1 no-outlier series and check shape (550,), no NaNs/infs, empirical sd close to 0.05 after rescaling, and that μ1 is not constant.
Run one series through c1_runner.py and check rejection flags are boolean and have length 500 after excluding the first n=50 observations.
Inspect one GEV calibration: quantile finite, shape parameter not absurd, rolling maxima count equals n-r+1 for r=floor(sqrt(50))=7, and selected bandwidth h is one of the grid values.
Check the full-run denominator is 1000*(11*50-50)=500,000 test points for C1; expected non-rejections at 98.3% is about 491,500.

Run a sanity baseline on 10-20 series before the full run: no-outlier specificity should be high (roughly >95%); if it is near 0% or 100%, suspect reversed GEV shape sign, wrong quantile, including first n in the metric, or a broken bandwidth CV.

Check the distribution of CV-selected bandwidths across a small subset; if essentially all at the grid boundary, note it and use the authors' default grid if available rather than expanding the grid ad hoc.
Before the full run, time the smoke run and estimate full runtime as (n_series/smoke_n_series) times smoke per-series cost; adjust workers to keep within budget.
budget_plan: Setup (clone if needed, pip install, import shim inspection): ~5-8 minutes. Smoke run (5 series): ~2-3 minutes. Full C1 run (1000 series, n=50, horizon=550): ~15-25 minutes with 8-16 workers, or ~25-30 minutes single-process if multiprocessing is unstable. Aggregation and metrics.json: ~1 minute. Keep ~5 minutes buffer for import issues and tolerance diagnostics. Do not start optional C2-C5 until C1 has produced metrics.json inside tolerance and at least ~15 minutes remain; C6-C8 are explicitly skipped in this budget because they require external BOM data.

nerally, Ca2018 seems unable to detect outliers reliably, when the errors
are uniformly distributed. Note that this is the only setting, where the data is in the
domain of attraction of the Weibull distribution.
Regarding other error processes, the results generally coincide, with some notable
exceptions. First, the specificity of our “partial” method is higher for independent errors
compared to AR errors and slightly higher compared to MA errors. For the latter error
processes, an extreme non-outlier value can propagate through time and lead to multiple
rejected null hypotheses. For small sample sizes, the “partial” method’s sensitivity is
higher for uniform errors, the stronger their dependence. Contrarily, the sensitivity of
the “full” method decreases with a stronger dependence.
In summary, the ML-based methods We2024, Ma2015 and Mu2018 seem to be overly
conservative with sensitivities substantially smaller than 5%. This issue likely results
from the Bonferroni correction, which is used to bound the familywise error rate of n
sequential tests to α. Further, the neural networks cannot be trained well in this setting
with low samples sizes, ranging from 50 to 200. A possible remedy for the difficulty of
training neural networks with short time series, might be the use of functional neural
networks that have fewer parameters and are known to work reasonably well, when data
is sparse (Heinrichs et al., 2023). Generally, the proposed testing procedures and Ca2018
yield similarly accurate results, where the higher sensitivity of the former balances out
the higher specificity of the latter. Note, however, that Ca2018 is a fully retrospective
method and cannot be used in an online fashion. Further, our “partial” method seems

tions. First, the specificity of our “partial” method is higher for independent errors
compared to AR errors and slightly higher compared to MA errors. For the latter error
processes, an extreme non-outlier value can propagate through time and lead to multiple
rejected null hypotheses. For small sample sizes, the “partial” method’s sensitivity is
higher for uniform errors, the stronger their dependence. Contrarily, the sensitivity of
the “full” method decreases with a stronger dependence.
In summary, the ML-based methods We2024, Ma2015 and Mu2018 seem to be overly
conservative with sensitivities substantially smaller than 5%. This issue likely results
from the Bonferroni correction, which is used to bound the familywise error rate of n
sequential tests to α. Further, the neural networks cannot be trained well in this setting
with low samples sizes, ranging from 50 to 200. A possible remedy for the difficulty of
training neural networks with short time series, might be the use of functional neural
networks that have fewer parameters and are known to work reasonably well, when data
is sparse (Heinrichs et al., 2023). Generally, the proposed testing procedures and Ca2018
yield similarly accurate results, where the higher sensitivity of the former balances out
the higher specificity of the latter. Note, however, that Ca2018 is a fully retrospective
method and cannot be used in an online fashion. Further, our “partial” method seems
to be slightly favorable compared to the “full” version.

rology. We considered daily temperature data from eight Australian cities, spanning

have been studied in the literature, and the null hypothesis of a stationary mean can be
rejected for all cities, but Gunnedah, at level α = 5%, even when seasonality is taking
into account (Bücher et al., 2020).

#
# repo_compat.py
#
# Compatibility shim so that the authors' repository (repo/) can be imported on
# machines where the optional competitor-method stacks (rpy2/R, river,
# tensorflow) are not installed.
#
# The target claim C1 only needs the proposed method ("Ours (full)"), which is
# pure NumPy/SciPy.  However `experiments.py` imports `alternative_methods`
# at module level, and that module imports rpy2 / river / tensorflow and even
# calls R at import time (`ro.r('library(envoutliers)')`).  We therefore insert
# lightweight placeholder modules into sys.modules *before* importing
# `experiments`.  The placeholders only raise if a competitor method is
# actually called, which never happens for C1 (we pass methods=[]).
#

import sys
import types


class _UnavailableDependency(Exception):
    pass


def _make_module(name):
    mod = types.ModuleType(name)
    mod.__dict__["__all__"] = []
    sys.modules[name] = mod
    return mod


def _stub_attr(mod, attr):
    def _fail(*args, **kwargs):
        raise _UnavailableDependency(
            f"{attr} from the optional competitor-method stack "
            f"({mod.__name__}) is not installed; it is not needed for the "
            "reproduced claim (only the proposed method is used)."
        )
    _fail.__name__ = str(attr)
    mod.__dict__[attr] = _fail
    return _fail


def _fake_ro_r(expr=""):
    # Mimics rpy2's `ro.r('library(envoutliers)')` at import time.
    return None


def install():
    """Install placeholder modules for the optional dependencies."""
    if "river" not in sys.modules:
        river = _make_module("river")
        for sub in ["anomaly", "linear_model", "optim", "preprocessing",
                    "time_series"]:
            _make_module(f"river.{sub}")
            setattr(river, sub, sys.modules[f"river.{sub}"])
        for sub in ["anomaly", "linear_model", "optim", "preprocessing",
                    "time_series"]:
            _stub_attr(sys.modules[f"river.{sub}"], "use")

    if "rpy2" not in sys.modules:
        rpy2 = _make_module("rpy2")
        robjects = _make_module("rpy2.robjects")
        rpy2.robjects = robjects
        robjects.r = _fake_ro_r
        robjects.FloatVector = _stub_attr(robjects, "FloatVector")
        robjects.NULL = object()
        robjects.conversion = _make_module("rpy2.robjects.conversion")

    if "tensorflow" not in sys.modules:
        tf = _make_module("tensorflow")
        for attr in ["keras", "nn", "layers", "Model", "Sequential"]:
            _stub_attr(tf, attr)

    # `experiments.py` also imports `tueplots` (plotting style helpers) which is
    # only used inside plotting functions.  Provide a stub if it is missing.
    try:
        import tueplots  # noqa: F401
    except ImportError:
        tue = _make_module("tueplots")
        bundles = _make_module("tueplots.bundles")
        tue.bundles = bundles
        for name in ["icml2022", "neurips2021", "jmlr2022", "icml2023",
                     "agrs2020"]:
            _stub_attr(bundles, name)


install()

#
# c1_runner.py
#
# Thin wrapper around the authors' repository code (repo/) that reproduces the
# simulation cells of Table 1 / Table 2 of
#   "Sequential Outlier Detection in Non-Stationary Time Series"
#   (arXiv:2502.18038) for the proposed "full" method.
#
# Nothing about the estimator itself is re-implemented here: data generation,
# bandwidth selection by 5-fold CV, the one-sided local-linear + Jackknife
# estimator and the GEV quantile calibration are all taken from
#   repo/data_generation.py, repo/jackknife.py, repo/quantiles.py,
#   repo/experiments.py.
#
# Mapping of paper terminology to the authors' code (verified against the code):
#   paper "Ours (full)"    -> repo mode 'parallel'   (experiments.parallel_test)
#   paper "Ours (partial)" -> repo mode 'sequential' (experiments.sequential_test)
# Rationale: the paper defines the "full" version as the estimator that uses
# *all* observations up to time i, whereas the "partial" version additionally
# discards observations that were already flagged as outliers.  In the code only
# `sequential_test` maintains such an `outlier_mask` (built from previously
# rejected points), while `parallel_test` uses every observation.  Hence
# 'parallel' == "full" and 'sequential' == "partial".
#

import os
import sys

import numpy as np

REPO_DIR = os.path.join(os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__)), "repo")
if REPO_DIR not in sys.path:
    sys.path.insert(0, REPO_DIR)

import repo_compat  # noqa: E402  (installs stubs for optional deps)
repo_compat.install()

import experiments  # noqa: E402
import data_generation  # noqa: E402
from jackknife import bandwidth_cv, jackknife_estimation  # noqa: E402
from quantiles import get_quantile  # noqa: E402

# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Configuration taken from the paper / the authors' config files.
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

SIGMA = 1 / 20            # errors rescaled to sd = 1/20 (Sec. 3.1, R14)
N_FACTOR = 11             # horizon = 11 * n (Sec. 3.1)
ALPHA = 0.01              # joint level for the n consecutive tests (Sec. 3.1, R10)
CV_KWARGS = {"num_folds": 5, "min_bw": 2, "max_bw": 20}   # 5-fold CV (R9)
OUTLIER_RATE = 0.05       # 5% of the observations (R11)


def _seeded_rng(seed):
    """
    Return a context manager that makes the stochastic parts of the authors'
    code reproducible.

    `data_generation.generate_iid` calls `np.random.default_rng()` *without* a
    seed, so we temporarily replace that factory by one that always returns the
    same seeded generator.  The legacy global RNG (`np.random.*`) is seeded as
    well because `bandwidth_cv` shuffles its CV folds with
    `np.random.shuffle`.  The order of random draws is fixed because the whole
    batch of time series is generated in a single vectorized call, so the run
    is deterministic.
    """

    class _Ctx:
        def __init__(self):
            self._orig = np.random.default_rng
            self._gen = np.random.default_rng(seed)

        def _factory(self, *args, **kwargs):
            if not args and not kwargs:
                return self._gen
            return self._orig(*args, **kwargs)

        def __enter__(self):
            np.random.seed(seed % (2 ** 32))
            np.random.default_rng = self._factory
            return self

        def __exit__(self, *exc):
            np.random.default_rng = self._orig
            return False

    return _Ctx()


def build_data_kwargs(mean_type, error_type, distribution, n_total, n_series):
    """Keyword arguments for the authors' `data_generation.generate_data`."""
    mean_kwargs = {"n": n_total}
    if mean_type == "1":
        mean_kwargs["a"] = 1.0                      # mu_1 as in repo config
    elif mean_type == "abrupt":
        mean_kwargs["cp"] = 0.5

    error_kwargs = {"n": n_total, "n_samples": n_series,
                    "sigma": SIGMA, "distribution": distribution}
    if error_type in ("ar", "ma"):
        error_kwargs = {"n": n_total, "n_samples": n_series, "sigma": SIGMA,
                        "error_dist": distribution}

    return {"mean_type": mean_type, "mean_kwargs": mean_kwargs,
            "error_type": error_type, "error_kwargs": error_kwargs}


def minimal_height(m_stable, distribution, std=SIGMA):
    """Distribution specific minimal outlier height (repo experiments_config)."""
    return experiments.get_minimal_height(m_stable, distribution, std=std)


def run_cell(m_stable=50, n_series=1000, mean_type="1", error_type="iid",
             distribution="normal", outlier=False, alpha=ALPHA,
             cv_kwargs=None, seed=0, modes=("parallel",), quiet=True):
    """
    Run one simulation cell of the paper's Table 1 / Table 2 with the proposed
    method and return the raw per-series results.

    :return: dict with keys per mode: 'reject_null' (bool array
        (n_series, 11*n - n)), 'bandwidth', 'quantile' plus the pooled counts.
    """
    n_total = N_FACTOR * m_stable
    m_remaining = n_total - m_stable
    cv_kwargs = dict(cv_kwargs or CV_KWARGS)

    data_kwargs = build_data_kwargs(mean_type, error_type, distribution,
                                    n_total, n_series)
    quantile_kwargs = {"alpha": alpha * np.ones(m_remaining),
                       "return_estimates": True}

    outlier_kwargs = None
    if outlier:
        outlier_kwargs = {
            "min_height": minimal_height(m_stable, distribution),
            "n_outliers": int(m_remaining * OUTLIER_RATE),
        }

    with _seeded_rng(seed):
        results = experiments.experiment(
            data_kwargs, m_stable, cv_kwargs, quantile_kwargs,
            outlier_kwargs=outlier_kwargs, methods=[], modes=list(modes))

    out = {"m_stable": m_stable, "n_total": n_total, "m_remaining": m_remaining,
           "n_series": n_series, "alpha": alpha, "outlier": outlier,
           "seed": seed, "modes": list(modes), "results": results}
    return out

#!/usr/bin/env python
"""
Reproduce the simulation results of

    F. Heinrichs, P. Bastian, H. Dette,
    "Sequential Outlier Detection in Non-Stationary Time Series" (arXiv:2502.18038)

Matched target claim: C1 -- empirical specificity of the proposed "full" method
for IID standard-normal errors (rescaled to mean 0 / sd 1/20), mean function mu1
and n = 50, over 1,000 simulated no-outlier time series of horizon 11n = 550.

The estimator itself (one-sided local linear + Jackknife, 5-fold CV bandwidth,
GEV quantile from the initial outlier-free period) is *not* re-implemented here;
it is taken verbatim from the authors' repository in ./repo via `c1_runner.py`.

Usage
-----
    python reproduce.py            # all simulation cells (C1 first), 1000 series
    python reproduce.py --smoke    # 5 series per cell, flow check only
    python reproduce.py --only C1  # single cell
    python reproduce.py --search   # small robustness sweep (GEV block size etc.)

Writes results/metrics.json.
"""

import argparse
import json
import os
import sys
import time

import numpy as np

import c1_runner as R

HERE = os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__))
RESULTS_DIR = os.path.join(HERE, "results")

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Simulation cells of Table 1 (no outliers) and Table 2 (5% outliers) that we
# reproduce.  `reference` is the value printed in the paper's table and is used
# ONLY for the comparison at the end -- it is never fed back into the method.
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
CELLS = {
    "C1": dict(claim="C1", metric="specificity", m_stable=50, outlier=False,
               reference=98.3, table="Table 1, Panel A (Specificity for mu1)",
               description="Ours (full), IID N(0,1) errors, mu1, n=50, no outliers"),
    "C2": dict(claim="C2", metric="specificity", m_stable=200, outlier=False,

    "C3": dict(claim="C3", metric="sensitivity", m_stable=50, outlier=True,
               reference=80.4, table="Table 2, Panel E (Sensitivity for mu1)",
               description="Ours (full), IID N(0,1) errors, mu1, n=50, 5% outliers"),
    "C4": dict(claim="C4", metric="sensitivity", m_stable=200, outlier=True,
               reference=97.5, table="Table 2, Panel E (Sensitivity for mu1)",
               description="Ours (full), IID N(0,1) errors, mu1, n=200, 5% outliers"),
    "C5": dict(claim="C5", metric="specificity", m_stable=50, outlier=True,
               reference=86.8, table="Table 2, Panel A (Specificity for mu1)",
               description="Ours (full), IID N(0,1) errors, mu1, n=50, 5% outliers"),
    "C6": dict(claim="C5", metric="specificity", m_stable=200, outlier=True,
               reference=87.2, table="Table 2, Panel A (Specificity for mu1)",
               description="Ours (full), IID N(0,1) errors, mu1, n=200, 5% outliers"),
    # Not a contract claim: the paper's "Ours (partial)" row of Table 1 Panel A
    # (n=50, N) is 97.9.  Running the repo's 'sequential' mode reproduces it and
    # thereby validates the full<->parallel / partial<->sequential mapping.
    "X_partial": dict(claim="X", metric="specificity", m_stable=50, outlier=False,
                      mode="sequential", reference=97.9,
                      table="Table 1, Panel A (Specificity for mu1)",
                      description="Ours (partial), IID N(0,1) errors, mu1, n=50, no outliers"),
}
DEFAULT_CELLS = ["C1", "C2", "C3", "C4", "C5", "C6", "X_partial"]


def run_cell(key, spec, n_series, seed, verbose=True):
    mode = spec.get("mode", "parallel")
    t0 = time.time()
    out = R.run_cell(m_stable=spec["m_stable"], n_series=n_series,
                     mean_type="1", error_type="iid", distribution="normal",
                     outlier=spec["outlier"], alpha=R.ALPHA, seed=seed,
                     modes=(mode,))
    dt = time.time() - t0
    summary = R.summarize(out, mode)
    est = out["results"][f"Estimates ({mode})"]

    # Per-series decisions for the audit trail.
    rej = out["results"][f"Ours ({mode})"]
    per_series = dict(
        rejection_rate=np.asarray(rej[0], dtype=float),
        fp=np.asarray(rej[1][:, 1, 0], dtype=int),
        tn=np.asarray(rej[1][:, 1, 1], dtype=int),
        tp=np.asarray(rej[1][:, 0, 0], dtype=int),
        fn=np.asarray(rej[1][:, 0, 1], dtype=int),
    )

    value = summary[f"{spec['metric']}_percent"]
    result = dict(
        claim=spec["claim"],
        description=spec["description"],
        table=spec["table"],
        metric=spec["metric"],
        mode=mode,
        n=spec["m_stable"],
        horizon=R.N_FACTOR * spec["m_stable"],
        test_points_per_series=R.N_FACTOR * spec["m_stable"] - spec["m_stable"],
        n_series=n_series,
        outlier=spec["outlier"],
        alpha=R.ALPHA,
        seed=seed,
        value=float(value),
        reference=spec["reference"],
        abs_diff=abs(float(value) - spec["reference"]),
        counts={k: summary[k] for k in ("tp", "fp", "fn", "tn")},
        mean_rejection_rate=summary["mean_rejection_rate"],
        gev_estimates=dict(mu_mean=est[0], mu_std=est[1], sigma_mean=est[2],
                           sigma_std=est[3], gamma_mean=est[4], gamma_std=est[5]),
        runtime_seconds=dt,
    )
    if verbose:
        print(f"[{key}] {spec['description']}: {spec['metric']} = "
              f"{value:.2f}% (paper {spec['reference']}%, "
              f"diff {result['abs_diff']:.2f}) in {dt:.1f}s")
    return result, per_series

def get_minimal_height(n: int, distribution: str) -> float:
    """
    Calculates minimal outlier height so that the test is consistent.

    :param n: Length of stable period.
    :param distribution: Error distribution.
        - The dominating sequences are:
        - 'normal': a_n= \sqrt{2 \log(n)}
        - 'uniform': b_n = 1 - 1/n
        - 'exponential': b_n = \log(n) / \lambda
        - 'pareto'/'pareto_infinite_variance': a_n = n^{1/a}
        - See: http://thierry-roncalli.com/download/HFRM-Chap12.pdf Table 12.4
        and Example 127
    :return: Minimal height.
    """

    if distribution == 'normal':
        c_n = np.sqrt(2 * np.log(n))
    elif distribution == 'uniform':
        c_n = 1 - 1/n
    elif distribution == 'exponential':
        c_n = np.log(n)
    elif distribution == 'pareto':
        c_n = n ** (1 / 4)
    elif distribution == 'pareto_infinite_variance':
        c_n = np.sqrt(n)
    else:
        raise ValueError(f"{distribution=} unknown.")

    # Factor originally so that minimal height was log(n)/10 for normal dist.
    factor = np.sqrt(np.log(n) / 200)

    return factor * c_n

def direct(m_stable, n_series, min_height, mode, seed=0, alpha=0.01):

             distribution="normal", outlier=False, alpha=ALPHA,
             cv_kwargs=None, seed=0, modes=("parallel",),
             outlier_height=None, quantile_extra=None):
    """
    Run one simulation cell of the paper's Table 1 / Table 2 with the proposed
    method and return the raw per-series results.

    :param outlier_height: override the distribution specific minimal outlier
        height (default: the authors' `get_minimal_height` from
        experiments_config_v2).  Used only by the `--search` robustness sweep.
    :param quantile_extra: extra keyword arguments forwarded to
        `quantiles.get_quantile` (e.g. block size / maxima method).
    :return: dict with the raw `experiments.experiment` results plus metadata.
    """
    n_total = N_FACTOR * m_stable
    m_remaining = n_total - m_stable
    cv_kwargs = dict(cv_kwargs or CV_KWARGS)

    data_kwargs = build_data_kwargs(mean_type, error_type, distribution,
                                    n_total, n_series)
    quantile_kwargs = {"alpha": alpha * np.ones(m_remaining),

    outlier_kwargs = None

        }

    with _seeded_rng(seed):
        results = experiments.experiment(
            data_kwargs, m_stable, cv_kwargs, quantile_kwargs,
            outlier_kwargs=outlier_kwargs, methods=[], modes=list(modes))

    out = {"m_stable": m_stable, "n_total": n_total, "m_remaining": m_remaining,
           "n_series": n_series, "alpha": alpha, "outlier": outlier,
           "seed": seed, "modes": list(modes),
           "outlier_kwargs": outlier_kwargs, "quantile_kwargs": quantile_kwargs,
           "results": results}
    return out

def get_quantile(X: np.ndarray, alpha: float | np.ndarray,
                 block_size: int = None, method: str = 'sliding',
                 return_estimates: bool = False) -> np.float64 | tuple:
    """
    Estimate 1-alpha quantile(s) based on a given dataset.

    :param X: One-dimensional data as NumPy array of size (n_timeseries, n) or
        (n,).
    :param alpha: Level of quantile to estimate, given as float or NumPy array.
    :param block_size: Number of elements to consider for each block maximum.
    :param method: String indicating 'sliding' or 'disjoint' block maxima.
    :param return_estimates: Boolean indicating whether to return estimates or
        only the quantile.
    :return: Estimated 1-alpha quantile(s), and possibly estimates mu, sigma and
        gamma.
    """
    n = X.shape[-1]

    if block_size is None:
        block_size = np.ceil(np.sqrt(n)).astype('int')

    block_maxima = get_block_maxima(X=X, block_size=block_size, method=method)
    gamma, sigma_r, mu_r = get_estimators(block_maxima)

    block_maxima_2 = get_block_maxima(X=X, block_size=2 * block_size,
                                      method=method)
    _, _, mu_2r = get_estimators(block_maxima_2)

    coeff = np.ones_like(gamma) * np.log(n / block_size) / np.log(2)
    ind = np.abs(gamma) > 1e-10
    coeff[ind] = ((n / block_size) ** gamma[ind] - 1) / (2 ** gamma[ind] - 1)

    sigma = sigma_r * (n / block_size) ** gamma
    mu = mu_r + (mu_2r - mu_r) * coeff

    if isinstance(alpha, float):
        alpha = np.array([[alpha]])
    elif isinstance(alpha, np.ndarray) and len(alpha.shape) == 1:
        alpha = np.expand_dims(alpha, axis=0)

    mu = np.expand_dims(mu, axis=-1)
    sigma = np.expand_dims(sigma, axis=-1)
    gamma = np.expand_dims(gamma, axis=-1)

    quantile = mu - sigma * np.log(- np.log(1 - alpha))
    quantile[ind] = mu[ind] + sigma[ind] / gamma[ind] * (
            (- np.log(1 - alpha)) ** (-gamma[ind]) - 1)

    if return_estimates:
        return quantile, mu, sigma, gamma
    else:
        return quantile

def search(n_series, seed, workers=None):
    """
    Robustness sweep over the two implementation choices that the paper leaves
    open (GEV block maxima and the CV fold split).  Runs *separately* from the
    default pipeline and is only used to document sensitivity, never to pick a
    configuration that best matches the paper.
    """
    import quantiles as Q
    results = []
    base = dict(m_stable=50, n_series=n_series, seed=seed, modes=("parallel",))
    for method in ["sliding", "disjoint"]:
        out = R.run_cell(**base)
        s = R.summarize(out, "parallel")
        results.append(dict(gev_block_maxima=method,
                            specificity_percent=s["specificity_percent"]))
        print("search", method, s["specificity_percent"])
    for shuffle in [True, False]:
        cv = dict(R.CV_KWARGS)
        cv["shuffle"] = shuffle
        out = R.run_cell(**base, cv_kwargs=cv)
        s = R.summarize(out, "parallel")
        results.append(dict(cv_shuffle=shuffle,
                            specificity_percent=s["specificity_percent"]))
        print("search shuffle", shuffle, s["specificity_percent"])
    for alpha in [0.005, 0.01, 0.02, 0.05]:
        out = R.run_cell(**base, alpha=alpha)
        s = R.summarize(out, "parallel")
        results.append(dict(alpha=alpha,
                            specificity_percent=s["specificity_percent"]))
        print("search alpha", alpha, s["specificity_percent"])
    path = os.path.join(HERE, "selected_config.json")
    with open(path, "w") as f:
        json.dump({"note": "default configuration is the paper's (alpha=1%, "
                           "sliding block maxima, repo default CV); this file "
                           "records a robustness sweep only",
                   "n_series": n_series, "seed": seed, "sweep": results}, f,
                  indent=2)
    print("wrote", path)
    return results

target.statement: Empirical specificity of the proposed full method for IID standard normal errors, mean function μ1, and n=50.
target.dataset: Simulated IID standard normal time series, mean function μ1, n=50, no outliers
target.table_ref: Table 1, Panel A (Specificity for μ1), row Ours (full), n=50, column N

tolerance.why: Rule 2: this is an accuracy-like % metric evaluated over 1,000 series × 550 time points (well over 2,000 observations), and the paper prints it as a percentage.

audit_summary: Target C1 is sound: the clean rerun computes 98.353% specificity on 1,000 no-outlier series (500,000 test points) using the authors' repo estimator, matching the paper's 98.3% within the 1.0 pp tolerance; paper numbers appear only in post-hoc reference fields, not in the computation. Fidelity is strong for the proposed method: one-sided local-linear smoothing with Jackknife, quartic kernel, 5-fold CV, GEV calibration from the first n points, constant alpha=1%, and full=parallel mapping (validated by the partial=sequential cross-check). Two caveats: the GEV estimator is the repo's block-maxima beta estimator rather than the ledger's MLE, and the bandwidth grid is the repo's integer 2..20 rather than the ledger's t-unit grid; both are paper-underspecified. The extra C3 n=50 contaminated sensitivity is 76.63% vs 80.4%, which is too large for seed noise with ~25k outlier points and likely reflects the unspecified outlier-height/placement assumption (A7); C2/C4/C5 match closely. The real-data claims C6-C8 were not attempted (disclosed), and the extra-cell labeled 'C6' is actually a C5 n=200 specificity cell, not contract C6. No anti-cheat or scale-down issue for the target; right_experiment is true.

requirement_check.evidence: c1_runner.run_cell builds data through the authors' data_generation with mean_type='1', error_type='iid', distribution='normal'; outlier_kwargs are supplied only for contaminated cells, so C1 has c_i=0 and C3/C5 add c_i!=0.
The target uses experiments.parallel_test via c1_runner; the repo's one-sided local-linear smoother with quartic kernel support [-1,0] is used, as recorded in the metrics config.
c1_runner imports jackknife_estimation; the recorded estimator is 2*hat_mu_{h/sqrt2}-hat_mu_h, i.e. the paper's Jackknife bias reduction.
experiments.experiment consumes quantiles.get_quantile with alpha=0.01 vector; decisions are based on |Xi - tilde_mu| exceeding the GEV (1-alpha) quantile.

GEV calibration is from the initial period, but the implementation uses the authors' repo sliding-block-maxima 'Books-Zanger beta-estimators' rather than the ledger's MLE/scipy fit; the paper permits MLE or PWM as examples and does not pin down the estimator. This is a fidelity caveat, not a target failure.
For C1 all 11n points are outlier-free; for contaminated cells c1_runner passes m_stable=50/200 as the initial period used for GEV calibration, and the repo experiment treats that period as stable.
c1_runner sets alpha=0.01 constant for all tests (alpha*np.ones(m_remaining)), matching the paper's constant-alpha Corollary 8(i) setup.
The repo smoother uses the one-sided quartic kernel with support [-1,0]; metrics config explicitly records this kernel for C1.
5-fold CV is used (CV_KWARGS num_folds=5) minimizing MSE. Caveat: the bandwidth grid is the repo's integer grid 2..20, not the ledger's t-unit grid; the paper does not specify the grid.
ALPHA=0.01 is passed as the per-test/joint level for the n consecutive tests.

Contaminated cells use OUTLIER_RATE=0.05 and n_outliers=int(m_remaining*0.05); target C1 has no outliers. Exact denominator (post-initial points) is an assumption but consistent with the outlier-free initial period.
Each executed simulation cell used 1,000 series: C1 uses 1,000 no-outlier series, and the contaminated mu1/IID-normal cells use 1,000 outlier series.

'Ours (full)' is mapped to repo 'parallel' (experiments.parallel_test), which uses all observations up to time i; the 'partial' cross-check (sequential, drops flagged points) gives 97.83% vs paper 97.9%, validating the mapping.
SIGMA=1/20 is passed to data_generation; IID normal errors have mean 0 and are rescaled to sd 1/20.
The Hobart/Melbourne BOM real-data claims C6-C8 were not attempted; results/metrics.json notes they need an external download and are outside the matched target.
